title: Implement Insertion Sort: pick each element and insert it in its correct position in the already sorted part; O(n^2) but fast for nearly sorted data.
keyPoints: Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix by inserting each new element into its correct place, shifting larger ones right.
It is adaptive: O(n) on nearly sorted data because few shifts are needed when elements are close to their final positions.
Time is O(n^2) in the worst case (reverse sorted); space is O(1); the algorithm is stable.
Stability comes from using strictly-greater-than when shifting, so equal elements are never moved past each other.
It is the practical winner among simple sorts for small arrays due to tiny constant factors and no recursion.
TimSort and introsort use insertion sort as the base case for subarrays below a threshold of about 10-20 elements.
It models the natural process of inserting new items into an already-sorted sequence one at a time.

s1_definition.oneliner: Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix by inserting each new element into its correct place, shifting bigger ones aside.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Insertion sort** – builds the sorted array one element at a time by taking the next unsorted element and inserting it into its correct position.
- **Shifting** – larger elements in the sorted prefix are shifted one step right to make room for the new element.
- **Adaptive** – runs in O(n) on nearly sorted data because few shifts are needed.
- **Stable** – the strictly-greater-than comparison during shifting preserves the order of equal elements.
- **Base case** – used inside TimSort and introsort for subarrays below a threshold of about 10-20 elements.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a clerk at the National Bank of India sorting a hand of balance cards the way you sort playing cards. She holds a sorted group in her left hand and picks up the next card with her right. She slides that card leftward past every card bigger than it until it sits in the right spot, then picks up the next one. The left hand is always sorted; each new card is simply inserted where it belongs.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Insertion sort builds the sorted array one element at a time. It takes each next element as a key and inserts it into its correct position within the sorted prefix by shifting every larger element one step right. It uses O(1) extra space and is stable because it uses strictly-greater-than when shifting.

Its signature strength is adaptivity. On nearly sorted data the inner loop does almost no work, giving O(n) time. This is why production sorts like TimSort use insertion sort as the base case for small subarrays below about 10-20 elements, where its tiny constant factors beat the O(n log n) sorts.

In a banking system at the National Bank of India, insertion sort models the natural process of maintaining a running sorted list as new transactions arrive one at a time. Each new amount is close to its final position, so insertion is fast.

The weakness is large, randomly ordered data, where the backward shifts dominate and it degrades to O(n^2). For general-purpose sorting, always use the library sort.

Remember one sentence: insertion sort slides each new element into its correct place in the sorted prefix, excelling on nearly sorted and small data because few shifts are needed.
